⭐️ BlackRock wants tokenized funds to back traditional Wall Street trades 

📣 BlackRock has identified the use of tokenized investment funds as trading collateral in traditional financial markets as a potential next application for blockchain technology, building on existing arrangements that already allow institutional crypto traders to pledge tokenized fund holdings. Dan Maley, BlackRock’s head of cash management for Asia Pacific, said the firm’s tokenized funds are already being used as collateral in digital-asset markets. Extending that capability into conventional financial markets remains more complicated, although the asset manager sees opportunities for investors to transfer fund holdings without first redeeming them for cash.

🔔 The development moves BlackRock’s discussion beyond issuing digital representations of traditional investment products. Its focus now includes how those assets could function within the systems financial institutions use to settle transactions, secure trading positions and manage available cash. Collateral plays an established role in financial markets because banks, brokers and clearing firms require assets to secure loans, derivatives positions and other transactions. Investors commonly provide cash or eligible securities, with each receiving institution setting rules for the assets it will accept.

🔗 BlackRock sees a potential role for tokenized money market fund shares in that process. A tokenized share represents an interest in an investment fund while allowing certain transactions involving that interest to take place through blockchain infrastructure. In the Bloomberg interview, Maley described the opportunity to bring tokenized funds into the traditional financial ecosystem. He distinguished the collateral arrangements already operating in cryptocurrency markets from the more difficult work of connecting blockchain-based assets with established financial systems.

Lately, I've been interviewing AI Engineer candidates with 1–2 years of experience.

One thing surprised me.
Almost everyone can talk about RAG.
Almost everyone has built AI agents.

Most have used LangChain, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, or Gemini.
But when the conversation moves beyond frameworks...
...that's where many interviews start to slow down.

I ask simple questions like:
"Why do embeddings work?"
"Why does chunk size affect retrieval?"
"Why does an attention mechanism matter?"
"What actually happens before an LLM generates the first token?"

The room usually goes quiet.
It made me realize something.
We're getting really good at building AI applications.

But we're slowly skipping the fundamentals that make those applications reliable.
AI tools can write code.
They can generate APIs.
They can even scaffold an entire project.

But they can't replace your understanding.
If retrieval quality drops...
If latency suddenly doubles...
If hallucinations increase...
If your AI agent gets stuck in a loop...

The solution isn't another framework.
It's understanding what's happening underneath.
Frameworks will change.
Models will change.
The fundamentals won't.

That's why, before every interview, I'd rather revise concepts like:
→ Transformers
→ Attention Mechanism
→ Embeddings
→ Tokenization
→ Vector Search
→ HTTP & APIs
→ System Design
→ Memory
→ Databases
→ Evaluation
→ Python fundamentals
These are the concepts that help you explain why something works, not just how to build it.

If you're preparing for AI Engineer interviews, don't spend all your time learning the next framework.
Spend some time strengthening the foundation that every framework is built on.

Some very troubling U.S. inflation data was released recently. PPI rose 6.3% year over year, versus expectations of 5.5%, and jumped 1.3% month over month, compared with forecasts of 0.6%. That’s the biggest monthly increase in producer prices since March 2022.

PPI shows how prices are changing for businesses themselves. When production, energy, transportation, and other costs go up, some of those increases are usually passed on to consumers over time. On top of that, the previous day’s consumer inflation report also came in hotter than expected. In other words, there have now been two consecutive signals that the U.S. inflation problem isn’t going away.

This is bad news for markets for a very simple reason. The higher inflation is, the less room the Fed has to cut rates, and the more likely interest rates are to stay elevated for longer. High rates are particularly painful for tech companies, crypto, and other assets that depend more heavily on cheap money and liquidity.

Part of the recent spike is indeed tied to energy prices, which jumped 10.8% in a single month. So it’s too early to call this a new inflation crisis based on one data point. But the problem is that price increases are showing up in other areas too, which means it’s not possible to blame everything on oil alone.

For Bitcoin over the long term, a single report doesn’t fundamentally change anything. But over the next few weeks, data like this increases the likelihood of pressure across the broader crypto market. The same goes for stocks, especially tech stocks.

That’s why it’s best not to rush into buying every dip right now. It makes more sense to keep some capital in cash and be prepared to buy quality assets at lower prices if the pressure continues. The long-term thesis remains unchanged, but in the short term, the market has one more reason to move lower.

The outcomes of the meeting of the IMF and World Bank leaders in Bangkok can be summarized in two words: "the global economy demonstrates resilience, but risks are increasing."

For those accustomed to systemic analysis, this phrase translates to: we are trying to prevent the system from collapsing, but the tools are becoming scarce and it will inevitably fail.

The word "resilience" is used in diplomatic language to conceal deep structural fragility or approaching the end.

There is fragmentation in global trade, reevaluation of supply chains, and the breaking of old financial ties. To call this resilience is to overlook the fact that the old architecture of globalization no longer works. And this is not unexpected; it is being intentionally and synchronously turned off right before our eyes.

Forecasts of a soft landing should be viewed with great skepticism. When global bankers start talking about resilience, it means that these risks have moved from the category of possible to the category of real.

Translating the reality into a cynical language: the world financial system may survive, but solely at your expense. When the IMF says that "the system is stable amid growing risks," they mean the structure will hold, but the occupants on the lower floors will be washed away by a tsunami.

The world is fracturing into warring regional blocs, which is a direct tax on the accustomed life that has already begun to be levied.

The era when an ordinary person could buy a Chinese gadget for pennies, fuel their car with cheap gasoline, and order cheap medicines from anywhere on the planet, is officially dead. Closed blocs mean scarcity, complicated logistics, and a total decline in quality with a doubling of prices.

Inflation is now the new norm, not a temporary crisis. To build new factories inside their blocs in place of the old unfriendly ones, governments will need trillions.

Where will they get them from? They will print them, diluting the purchasing power of your savings and salaries. Your money will melt before your eyes just for the system to simulate stability.

Resource nationalism is when the world shifts from competing for goods to a fierce struggle for survival and resources: chips, lithium, energy, and food. Access to them is now granted not for money, but for geopolitical loyalty.

And Russia, as a country with huge resources, as well as food and water, may soon dictate its terms to everyone else, providing access to them based on political motives and on its own terms, as is now happening with diesel fuel and gas.

Globally, we are headed towards an era of rich states and poor people. At the top, reports will tout the growth of the military-industrial complex and the stability of the banking sector, while people will go hungry due to the new prices on basic products.

The slogan "The economy is stable" is an attempt to convince the passengers of the sinking Titanic that the first class is still being served well, with fresh oysters, quail, and Moët & Chandon.

The main mistake today is to continue living with the financial habits of the affluent 2010s. Taking out mortgages, car loans, and planning decades ahead with incomes that may literally disappear tomorrow.

Anyone who does not adjust their plans to the reality of closed and expensive economic blocs right now will soon be looking for shelter.

Having a simple resource will be more advantageous than having a clever investment or career plan. These are the conclusions from the bankers' gathering in Bangkok.
